introduction: On this Sunday, Sirach asks how we can hope for God's forgiveness if we refuse to forgive others. In the Gospel, Peter asks how often he must forgive, and Jesus answers, Seventy times seven, and tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven a huge debt but would not forgive a small one. Paul tells us that whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. Let us forgive from our hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger and rich in compassion. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a school of forgiveness and mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For families, communities and nations divided by old hurts: that they may find the grace to forgive. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have been deeply wounded by others: that God may heal them and give them the strength to forgive. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who find it hard to accept God's forgiveness: that they may know how much they are forgiven. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may forgive our brothers and sisters from our hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful Father, you have forgiven us a debt we could never repay. Give us hearts that forgive others as you have forgiven us. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Seventy times seven
reflection.body:
Sirach speaks plainly: "Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray." He asks a pointed question: "Does anyone harbor anger against another and expect healing from the Lord?" We cannot ask God for mercy while refusing it to others.

In the Gospel, Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive: "Until seven times?" He thinks he is being generous. Jesus answers, "I don't tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven." In other words, without limit.

Then Jesus tells a parable. A servant owes his king an enormous debt, ten thousand talents, an amount no one could ever repay. He begs for patience, and the king, "being moved with compassion," forgives the entire debt. But the same servant then meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a small sum, grabs him by the throat and demands payment. When the fellow servant begs for patience, he refuses and has him thrown into prison.

The king summons him: "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Shouldn't you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?" Jesus concludes that the Father will treat us the same way "if you don't each forgive your brother from your hearts."

The parable shows the reason to forgive: we have been forgiven far more. Forgiveness does not mean pretending the hurt didn't happen, or that trust is immediately restored. It means letting go of the desire for revenge and leaving judgment to God.

This week, think of someone you have not forgiven. Pray for them by name. Ask God for the grace to forgive from your heart, even if it takes time. And remember how much you have been forgiven.
